subsection: 11. Culture: consensus and its collapse — Hollywood, the red scare, youth culture, counter-culture and multiculturalism

notes.h: Background: consensus, liberalism and mass media
notes.b: Historians often describe 1950s America as a society that broadly agreed on its core values, and then ask when and why that agreement broke down. Three ideas run through this subsection: consensus, liberalism and mass media.
points: Consensus means the shared values said to characterise the 1950s: prosperity, suburban family life and anti-communism in the Cold War (the rivalry with the Soviet Union). Historians argue about how real this agreement was, which is why the term matters in essays.

Liberalism, as used here, means support for civil liberties (freedoms such as speech and a fair hearing) and tolerance of difference. The 1950s tested it, for example in the red scare, and the 1960s movements tried to extend it to more groups.

Mass media means film, television, radio and print that reach a national audience. They helped create a common national culture in the 1950s, so a singer shown on national television could become famous across the country at once.
The same media later carried youth culture and protest to a national audience, which is why local scenes such as San Francisco's hippie district could become national symbols.

Fear of communism at home was already strong: Truman's loyalty programme (checks on the political loyalty of government employees) and McCarthyism (Senator McCarthy's accusations of communist infiltration) formed the wider mood in which Hollywood was investigated.

The 1960s protests grew out of three developments: the civil rights movement (the campaign for equal rights for black Americans), the Vietnam War, and Nixon's election as president in 1968, which brought a conservative reaction.

A counter-culture is a youth culture that deliberately rejects the dominant values of the society around it, while multiculturalism is the idea that a society contains many cultures, each with a claim to be recognised, rather than one American culture.
notes.tip: Judgement questions ask whether the 1950s were united and whether the 1960s broke that unity. Define consensus first, then use evidence from both decades.

notes.h: Hollywood and the American Dream on screen, 1945 to 1960
notes.b: In the postwar years a handful of studios dominated American film, and many of their films celebrated family, prosperity and patriotic values. Their power then weakened as the law and television changed the business.
points: The studio system meant that major companies such as MGM, Warner Brothers and Paramount controlled film production, distribution and cinemas. The Paramount decree (the Supreme Court's decision of 1948) ordered them to separate production from cinema ownership, and the sale of the chains followed over the next decade.

Frank Capra's It's a Wonderful Life (1946) set small-town community and decency against greed. It was disappointing at the box office on release but was widely shown on television from the 1970s and became a lasting image of the American Dream.

The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) dealt with returning veterans and won seven Academy Awards. Social-problem films (films about a social issue) also tackled anti-Semitism in Gentleman's Agreement (1947) and race in Pinky (1949).

Hollywood films of the 1950s increasingly addressed family life, race and juvenile delinquency (crime and misbehaviour by the young), showing that the studios were responding to the anxieties of the decade as well as to its optimism.
Television drew audiences away from cinemas from the early 1950s, so the studios began to sell films to television and to produce television series themselves.

Weekly cinema attendance peaked at about 90 million in 1946 and roughly halved by 1960. The studios fought back with spectacle that television could not match: wide-screen CinemaScope (1953), colour and epics such as The Ten Commandments (1956) and Ben-Hur (1959).

Musicals such as Singin' in the Rain (1952) and family comedies promoted cheerful abundance. The American Dream of home, family and consumption was the staple of studio films and of the new television comedies.

Westerns and science fiction carried Cold War messages. High Noon (1952) is often read as an allegory (a story with a hidden political meaning) of the blacklist, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) as a fable of conformity or of communist infiltration; both readings are interpretations.
notes.tip: A Hollywood question asks what the studios showed and how it reflected or shaped values. Name specific films with years, and cover the American Dream, Cold War messages, the red scare and television's challenge.

notes.h: The Production Code and its replacement by ratings
notes.b: Hollywood policed itself with a moral code that decided what could appear on screen. Its decline in the 1950s and 1960s shows changing attitudes in American culture.
points: The Production Code (Hollywood's own rulebook of what films could show) was enforced by the Hays Office from 1934, and it continued in the 1950s to restrict the treatment of sex and crime.
The Moon Is Blue (1953) was released without Code approval, which weakened the Code's authority because a film could succeed without it.
A ratings system, which labels films according to the audience they suit instead of cutting them to fit a code, replaced the Production Code in November 1968.

notes.b: From 1947 the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), a committee of the House of Representatives, investigated communist influence in the film industry. The result was a blacklist, a secret list of people whom employers refused to hire, which ended many careers.
points: HUAC opened hearings on communist influence in Hollywood in October 1947. The Hollywood Ten, screenwriters and directors who refused to answer questions, were convicted of contempt of Congress and sentenced in 1948; appeals delayed matters, and they served their prison terms from 1950.
The studios' Waldorf Statement of November 1947, in which studio heads pledged not to employ known communists, was their response to the hearings, and a blacklist operated for years afterwards.
Writers who could not work under their own names, such as Dalton Trumbo, kept writing by using pseudonyms or fronts (friends who put their own names on the scripts).
Kirk Douglas credited Trumbo on Spartacus and Otto Preminger did so on Exodus, both in 1960. Openly naming a blacklisted writer broke the blacklist and showed that the industry's rules were changing.

Friendly witnesses (those who cooperated with HUAC) included Ronald Reagan, then president of the Screen Actors Guild, and Walt Disney. In 1952 the director Elia Kazan named former communist colleagues, and he made On the Waterfront in 1954.
The human cost was large: hundreds of writers, actors and directors were blacklisted, and Charlie Chaplin left the United States in 1952 when his re-entry permit was withdrawn.
The studios also made anti-communist films, such as I Was a Communist for the FBI (1951), to prove their loyalty to a suspicious public.
notes.tip: Do not confuse HUAC's Hollywood hearings of 1947 with Senator McCarthy's Senate investigations of the 1950s, or the Hollywood Ten with the later witnesses. If asked for the red scare's results, give the blacklist and the ruined careers as dated points.

notes.h: Key personality: Marilyn Monroe (career, image and death)
notes.b: Marilyn Monroe was one of the biggest film stars of the 1950s. Her career shows how the studio system and the mass media created, sold and then used up a public image.
points: She was born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles in 1926. Her screen career began with small roles in the late 1940s, and The Asphalt Jungle and All About Eve (both 1950) brought wider fame.
She became a star in 1953 with Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and How to Marry a Millionaire. With The Seven Year Itch (1955) she was one of the most popular box office stars of the decade.

She studied at the Actors Studio in New York in the mid-1950s, and her marriage to the playwright Arthur Miller in 1956 linked her to serious drama, which suited her wish to be taken seriously as an actress.
Some Like It Hot (1959), directed by Billy Wilder, won critical praise and remains her most admired comedy. Her last completed film was The Misfits (1961), written by Miller.

She had disputes with studio executives over her contract and her choice of roles, and the press reported them widely. In June 1962 Twentieth Century-Fox dismissed her from Something's Got to Give after repeated absences.

Her glamorous image, spread by film, press and advertising, made her a public fascination and an example of mass media and consumer culture. Contemporaries judged her a glamorous star, while later critics argued that the studio system exploited women performers.
She sang "Happy Birthday, Mr President" to John F. Kennedy at a Democratic Party fundraiser at Madison Square Garden on 19 May 1962.

She died at her Los Angeles home on the night of 4 August 1962, aged 36, and was found early on 5 August. The cause was a barbiturate overdose, ruled a probable suicide, and the conspiracy theories that followed have no support in the official investigation.
notes.tip: Open with dated headline facts: the 1953 films that made her a star and her death on 4 August 1962. Give the cause only as a barbiturate overdose ruled a probable suicide, and do not confuse her death (1962) with Kennedy's assassination (1963).

notes.h: Youth culture and the beat generation, 1950s
notes.b: Teenagers became a distinct consumer group in the 1950s, and new music, films and writing challenged the conformity of the era. Mass media turned these youth tastes into a national phenomenon.
points: Teenagers now had money and leisure to spend on their own music, films and fashions, which made youth a commercial market that businesses set out to serve.

Rock and roll drew on black rhythm and blues (a style of black popular music) and reached white teenagers through radio and records. Bill Haley's Rock Around the Clock (1955) was one of its early hits.
Elvis Presley's Heartbreak Hotel (1956) was one of the first rock and roll national hits, and his appearances on the Ed Sullivan Show in 1956 and 1957 made rock and roll a national craze.

Dick Clark's American Bandstand, on the national network from 1957, turned youth culture into a commercial market. Older critics condemned the music as a threat to morals, an early example of a moral panic about the young.
The actor James Dean, who starred in Rebel Without a Cause (1955) and died in a car crash in September 1955, became a symbol of teenage alienation, as did Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953).
The Beat generation was a group of writers who rejected the conventions of suburban life. Allen Ginsberg's poem Howl was published in 1956, and Jack Kerouac's On the Road appeared in 1957.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Beats, who were 1950s writers, with the hippies of the 1960s counter-culture, or 1950s rock and roll with 1960s rock.

notes.b: Norman Mailer was a novelist, essayist and public figure whose writing and persona made him a central voice in the debate over American culture from the 1950s to the 1960s.
points: His first novel, The Naked and the Dead (1948), drew on his service in the Pacific during the Second World War and became a best seller. In 1955 he co-founded the Village Voice newspaper in New York, part of the counter-cultural press of the period.
His essay The White Negro (1957) argued that the hipster, who borrowed from black culture and lived for the moment, offered a model of rebellion against the conformity of postwar America.

The Armies of the Night (1968) covered the anti-war march on the Pentagon in October 1967. Mailer was arrested there and wrote about himself in the third person; the book won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award.
His public persona, including a campaign for mayor of New York in 1969, made him a celebrity as well as a literary authority, which meant that his self-promotion was part of his influence.

His later works included Miami and the Siege of Chicago (1968), The Fight (1975) about the boxers Ali and Foreman in Zaire, and The Executioner's Song (1979), which won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction.

Contemporaries were divided. Admirers saw a serious critic of American culture, while critics attacked his self-promotion, his machismo and his stabbing of his second wife Adele in 1960, for which he received a suspended sentence.
The White Negro was widely attacked for romanticising black life, and James Baldwin criticised Mailer for it, so even his admirers disputed its argument.
Historians today generally treat his non-fiction, especially The Armies of the Night, as an important account of the 1960s protest movement.
notes.tip: Examiners expect the three works with dates and the idea behind each: war, hipster rebellion and anti-war protest. Add a view on his public persona and his critics, and do not confuse The Naked and the Dead (1948) with The Armies of the Night (1968).

notes.b: Muhammad Ali's career linked sport, religion and the anti-war movement, which made him a symbol of black pride and of political resistance.
points: Born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942, he won Olympic light-heavyweight gold at Rome in 1960.
He won the world heavyweight title by beating Sonny Liston in Miami Beach on 25 February 1964. His saying float like a butterfly, sting like a bee summed up his boxing style.

In March 1964 he announced his membership of the Nation of Islam (a black American religious movement) and his new name. Its leader Elijah Muhammad gave him the name, and he rejected Clay as a slave name.

In 1966 he told reporters he had no quarrel with the Viet Cong. On 28 April 1967 he refused induction into the army in Houston as a Muslim minister and conscientious objector (one who refuses service on grounds of faith), and lost his title and licence.

In June 1967 he was convicted of draft evasion, sentenced to five years in prison and fined 10,000 dollars, but stayed free on appeal. The Supreme Court overturned the conviction on 28 June 1971 by 8 votes to 0 (Justice Marshall took no part).
He was barred from boxing for over three years and returned in October 1970. He lost to Joe Frazier in the Fight of the Century at Madison Square Garden on 8 March 1971.

He regained the title by beating George Foreman at Kinshasa, Zaire, on 30 October 1974 (the Rumble in the Jungle) and beat Frazier in the Thrilla in Manila in 1975. He retired in 1981 and lived with Parkinson's disease.

Contemporaries were sharply divided: many white Americans and sports writers condemned him, while many young black Americans and anti-war activists saw a principled leader. Historians such as David Remnick (King of the World, 1998) treat him as a symbol of black pride and of resistance to the Vietnam War.
notes.tip: Strong answers link sport, religion and politics: the name change, the draft refusal on grounds of faith, the penalty, the 1971 reversal, and why he became a symbol of black pride and of resistance to Vietnam. Say March 1964 for the name change, and do not confuse the 1967 conviction with the 1971 reversal.

notes.h: The counter-culture: Haight-Ashbury, drugs and music
notes.b: The late 1960s counter-culture rejected the consumer and corporate values of the 1950s. Hippies, young people who dropped out of conventional life, linked personal liberation to music, drugs and a new way of living.
points: The Summer of Love of 1967 drew thousands of young people to the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco, where a counter-culture of music, drugs and communal living developed.

Timothy Leary, a former Harvard psychologist, urged young people to turn on, tune in and drop out. The phrase is usually dated to his public use at the Human Be-In in San Francisco on 14 January 1967, though Leary says he coined it in 1966, so the date is contested.
LSD, a powerful hallucinogenic drug (one that alters perception), was banned in California in 1966, yet drug use remained a central part of the hippie scene.

Rock musicians such as Bob Dylan, Jimi Hendrix and the Beatles, whose Sgt Pepper album appeared in 1967, gave the movement its soundtrack, and the film Easy Rider (1969) put the counter-culture on screen.
notes.tip: Keep the three places apart: Haight-Ashbury (San Francisco, 1967), Woodstock (New York, 1969) and Altamont (California, 1969).

notes.h: The counter-culture: festivals, protest and backlash, 1968 to 1971
notes.b: The counter-culture had a political wing and a dramatic public stage, but it also provoked a reaction. Its limits matter as much as its fame.
points: The Woodstock music festival, held near Bethel, New York, from 15 to 18 August 1969, attracted about 400,000 people (estimates vary) and became a symbol of the generation.
The festival at Altamont Speedway in California in December 1969, where a man was killed by the Hells Angels during a Rolling Stones concert, was seen as the end of the dream of peace and love.
The Students for a Democratic Society and the Black Panther Party were among the political groups that drew on counter-cultural style and protest in the late 1960s.
The Yippies, led by Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, mixed theatre and politics, and took part in the protests at the Democratic Convention in Chicago in 1968.
Most young Americans were not hippies, so the counter-culture was a minority movement rather than the voice of a whole generation.

The counter-culture provoked a backlash among the silent majority, the phrase Nixon used in his speech of November 1969 to describe ordinary Americans who did not protest. He was elected in 1968 and re-elected in 1972.
notes.tip: If asked for the counter-culture's effects, give the backlash and the multicultural claims as separate, dated points, and note that most Americans were not hippies.

notes.b: In the 1960s and 1970s minority groups asserted their identities and demanded equal rights, challenging the idea of a single American culture.
points: The Chicano movement (the movement of Mexican Americans) was led in part by Cesar Chavez and the National Farm Workers Association, which organised farm workers in California from the early 1960s.

The Delano grape strike and boycott from 1965 won national support for Chavez. The 1966 merger with another union created the United Farm Workers Organizing Committee, which was renamed the United Farm Workers in 1972.
The American Indian Movement was founded in Minneapolis in 1968 to campaign against discrimination and for treaty rights.

American Indian activists occupied Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay from November 1969 until 1971, and AIM occupied Wounded Knee, South Dakota, in 1973; both were protests that drew national attention.

Black Power, the Black Panther Party and the black arts movement asserted pride in African American culture. The television series Roots (1977) drew about 100 million viewers for its final episode, showing how mass media reached a national audience with this theme.

notes.h: Multiculturalism: women, gay rights, the law and the end of consensus
notes.b: Women and gay Americans also organised in these years, and new laws made American society more diverse. Together these developments undermined the idea of one shared national culture.
points: The women's liberation movement disrupted the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City in September 1968, protesting the way women were presented to the public.

The Stonewall riots began on 28 June 1969 after a police raid on the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in Greenwich Village, New York. Organisations existed before 1969, so Stonewall is widely seen as a turning point in the gay rights movement rather than its beginning.
The Gay Liberation Front was founded shortly after Stonewall, and marches commemorating the riots began in 1970.
The Immigration Act of 1965 and the Bilingual Education Act of 1968 encouraged a more diverse society and gave a legal basis to minority languages in schools.
The concept of consensus, which historians used to describe the 1950s, was challenged as Americans debated race, gender, sexuality and national identity in the 1960s and 1970s.

notes.h: Assessment: did a consensus exist and did it collapse?
notes.b: Examiners reward judgements that test the idea of consensus against evidence of conflict within postwar culture. Both sides of the argument need dated evidence.
points: Supporters of the consensus view argue that most Americans shared a belief in prosperity, family and anti-communism in the 1950s, as shown by the popularity of the films and television of the period.
Critics of the consensus view argue that the 1950s were marked by conflict over race, sex and loyalty, and that the red scare shows the limits of the supposed consensus.
The 1960s counter-culture showed that a sizeable minority rejected the values of the 1950s, but the majority of Americans in 1968 still backed conventional candidates and the war.
Historians differ over whether the collapse of consensus was a sudden break around 1968 or a gradual shift that began with the civil rights movement in the 1950s.
notes.tip: Judgement questions reward answers that use both the counter-culture and the red scare as evidence, and that note that most Americans were not hippies.

keyTerms.definition: In the cultural context, the tradition of civil liberties and tolerance that the 1950s consensus tested, and which the 1960s protest movements extended to race, sex and sexuality.
Film, television, radio and print, which shaped the consensus of the 1950s and carried the images of youth culture and protest to a national audience.
The youth movement of the late 1960s that rejected mainstream values and linked personal freedom to political protest, centred on Haight-Ashbury and Woodstock.
The industry-wide list of writers, actors and directors refused work because of alleged communist sympathies, a practice that followed the Hollywood hearings of 1947.
The assertion in the 1960s and 1970s of the rights and identities of ethnic, racial and sexual minorities against a single model of American culture.
The historians' term for the shared values of prosperity, family and anti-communism that many saw as characteristic of American culture in the 1950s.
The writers, such as Kerouac and Ginsberg, who in the 1950s rejected suburban conformity and influenced the 1960s counter-culture.
The June 1969 protests in Greenwich Village, New York, after a police raid on a gay bar, which began the modern gay rights movement.
The film industry's self-censorship code, enforced by the Hays Office from 1934, which restricted the portrayal of sex and crime until it was replaced by a ratings system in 1968.
A member of the late 1960s counter-culture who rejected conventional dress, work and sexual morals and favoured communal living, drugs and music.
The black religious and political organisation led by Elijah Muhammad that Ali joined in 1964.
